40032.q: Refer to the graph. A student says a $6 minimum wage binds, fixes employment at 300 thousand and creates a 200-thousand-worker surplus. Which diagnosis corrects the claim and identifies the policy that could sustain the gap at $6?

Binding floor: $6 and 300 thousand; Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage ceiling.
Nonbinding floor: $12 and 200 thousand; at $6, Qs > Qd by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage floor.
Binding floor: $6 and 100 thousand; Qd > Qs by 200 thousand, consistent with a binding wage floor.
40032.imageAlt: The labor market has wage vertically and quantity in thousands of workers horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at 200 thousand workers and 12 dollars. A wage floor at 6 dollars intersects demand at 300 thousand and supply at 100 thousand.

At a hypothetical $6 wage, firms demand 300 thousand workers but only 100 thousand offer labor: a shortage, not surplus. A binding wage ceiling could prevent wage from rising; the floor does not.

42189.q: Refer to the coastal-protection graph and treat quantity as continuous. A council budgets $700 million to expand from 10 to 30 miles. With no fixed or financing costs, which assessment uses the changing marginal cost correctly?

The budget is sufficient: expansion costs $500 million and adds $300 million in net benefits.
The expansion costs $600 million because its final marginal cost applies to all 20 miles.

42189.feedback: MC rises from $20 million to $30 million per mile, so added cost is 20 x (20 + 30)/2 = $500 million. MSB falls from 50 to 30, giving added benefit 20 x (50 + 30)/2 = $800 million. Net gain is $300 million.

42197.q: The graph plots North and South MB at the same quantity of four displays. Which summation rule does this illustrate?

Private-good buyers must consume identical quantities

42322.q: The graph’s competitive equilibrium is $20 per hour. A binding wage floor holds wages at $30, where labor supplied exceeds labor demanded. If the floor is removed with both curves unchanged, which adjustment is consistent with the model?
options: The wage falls toward $20; labor demand shifts right and labor supply shifts left solely because the wage falls.
The wage rises above $30; excess labor supply indicates employers cannot recruit enough workers.
The wage falls toward $20; labor demanded rises and labor supplied falls along their existing curves.
The wage stays at $30; removing the floor changes only the label attached to unemployment.
42322.commonError: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
42322.feedback: At the enforced above-equilibrium wage there is excess labor supply. Removing it permits a lower wage, increasing hiring and reducing the quantity offered along unchanged curves until they meet.

42324.q: Refer to the graph above. How should the point where the two curves cross be interpreted?

It is one firm's profit-maximizing hiring point
It is the maximum possible workforce
It is the wage where worker productivity becomes zero
42324.commonError: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
42324.feedback: The graph represents an entire labor market. Its intersection balances aggregated firm demand with worker supply; it is not a single firm's VMP decision.

42325.q: At 6,000 workers in the graph, the wage required by labor supply exceeds firms’ marginal willingness to pay on labor demand. A proposal forces hiring up to that level without changing productivity or workers’ opportunity costs. Which marginal assessment is correct?
options: Every extra wage dollar is a net social gain, so hiring beyond the demand-supply intersection must raise surplus.
Some additional hires have opportunity cost above their marginal product value; wage payments alone do not establish a net social gain.
Marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost because labor supply lies above demand at 6,000.
No marginal comparison is possible because labor demand measures average rather than marginal product value.
42325.commonError: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
42325.feedback: Labor supply reflects workers’ marginal opportunity cost and demand their marginal product value in this competitive model. When supply lies above demand, forcing those extra hires uses resources worth more than the output they add.

42329.q: The graph marks employment at 40 on an axis measured in hundreds, with wage $20. A later equilibrium is 60 on the same scale at wage $25. An analyst reports payroll rises from $800 to $1,500, a 50% increase. Which correction is complete?
options: Payroll rises from $80,000 to $150,000, a 50% increase because only employment matters.
Payroll rises from $80,000 to $150,000, an 87.5% increase; both the axis scale and the wage change matter.
Payroll rises from $800 to $1,500, an 87.5% increase because the axis scale does not affect dollar totals.

42331.q: The graph moves from 4,000 warehouse workers at $20 to 6,000 at $25 with labor supply unchanged. A manager attributes the increase to more workers becoming available at every wage. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The manager is correct because any rise in employment must be a rightward labor-supply shift.
The graph shows movement down unchanged labor demand because the wage rose.
The graph shows lower labor demand because higher wages reduce firms’ desired employment at every wage.
The graph instead shows greater labor demand; employment rises despite a higher wage, while a supply expansion alone would tend to lower the wage.
42331.commonError: Reverses the wage or employment effect of a labor-demand shift.
42331.feedback: The new outcome has both higher wage and employment and is on the unchanged supply curve. A rightward demand shift accounts for both; a supply expansion alone has a different wage direction.

42334.q: The graph shows warehouse labor demand increasing. Suppose a sorting system raises marginal product by 25% at every employment level, but the competitive output price simultaneously falls by 10%. How does value of marginal product compare with its original level, and does that support the depicted demand shift?
options: It rises by 15%, supporting a rightward shift because the percentage changes should simply be subtracted.
It falls by 10%, contradicting the shift because product price alone determines labor demand.
It rises by 12.5%, supporting a rightward demand shift because 1.25×0.90=1.125.
It remains unchanged because a productivity gain and a price decline always cancel.
42334.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
42334.feedback: VMP is product price times marginal product. Combining the two changes gives 1.25×0.90=1.125, a 12.5% increase at each employment level, supporting increased labor demand.

42335.q: Refer to the graph above. Customer demand for next-day delivery rises. Why can the solid demand curve represent the resulting labor-market change?

More valuable warehouse output raises derived demand for workers
42335.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
42335.feedback: Labor demand is derived from demand for the services workers help produce. Stronger delivery demand can raise the value of workers' marginal product.

42337.q: The graph shows D L0 shifting to D L1 while labor supply stays fixed. A report says “the higher wage caused labor demand to increase.” Which sequence correctly separates cause from movement?
options: The higher wage shifts labor demand right; the extra employment then shifts labor supply left.
An increase in productivity or output demand raises labor demand; the resulting higher wage brings movement along unchanged labor supply.
The higher wage moves employers down their original demand curve; no demand shifter is required.
Labor supply shifts right first; the higher wage is the normal result of that supply expansion.
42337.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
42337.feedback: A wage change moves quantity demanded along a labor-demand curve; it does not shift that curve. A demand determinant changes first, and the new equilibrium includes movement along supply.

42341.q: The orchard graph shows employment falling from 4,000 to 2,000 after a productivity loss at unchanged output price. A later output-price increase raises marginal revenue product, but its size is not given. Which conclusion is defensible?
options: The first employment loss is 2,000; any later price rise necessarily restores exactly 4,000 workers.
The first employment loss is 2,000; the later price rise partly offsets the demand reduction, but the final employment level relative to 4,000 is not determined.
The first employment loss is 200; a higher output price shifts labor supply right rather than demand.
The first employment loss is 4,000; the later price rise cannot affect derived labor demand.
42341.commonError: Reverses the wage or employment effect of a labor-demand shift.
42341.feedback: Read the initial change with the hundreds-of-workers scale: 4,000−2,000=2,000. A higher output price raises product value per worker, opposing the original demand loss. Without the magnitude, restoration to or beyond the original level is uncertain.

42343.q: A disease reduces each orchard worker’s marginal product by 20%, but the fruit price rises by 25%. Assume competitive output pricing and the same percentage productivity effect at each employment level. Does the graph’s leftward labor-demand shift necessarily follow after both changes?

No; VMP rises by 5% because the percentage changes should be added algebraically.
Yes; the fruit-price rise lowers VMP by increasing workers’ opportunity cost.
No; VMP is unchanged because 0.80×1.25=1, so the productivity loss alone does not determine the combined labor-demand effect.
42343.commonError: Forgets that labor demand is derived from productivity and output-market conditions.
42343.feedback: Derived demand depends on price times marginal product. The stated price rise exactly offsets the productivity decline: 1.25×0.80=1. Neither effect can be considered alone.

42377.q: The monopsony graph shows hiring of 4,000 nurses at wage $20, where MFC=MRP=$30. The competitive intersection of supply and MRP is 6,000 at $25. Which comparison explains why expanding employment toward the competitive level can raise surplus despite a higher wage?

42577.q: With yogurt horizontal, its price doubles from $4 to $8 while cereal stays $8. Income then doubles from $40 to $80. Relative to the original budget, which claim correctly separates the income and relative-price effects?

The Gini falls by 12.8 income dollars per household, exactly offsetting the $2,000 income decline.
42741.feedback: The Gini change is 0.380−0.252=0.128; mean income falls 2,000/20,000=10%. Distribution and income level must be assessed separately.
42741.imageAlt: An after-policy Lorenz curve lies closer to equality than the before-policy curve; Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252.

42742.q: Refer to the graph above. What does the lower after-policy Gini imply?
options: Mean income must be higher
Poverty is eliminated
The after-policy distribution is more equal
Every household has the same income
42742.feedback: A lower Gini means the Lorenz curve is closer overall to equality, not necessarily that all gaps or poverty disappear.
42742.imageAlt: An after-policy Lorenz curve lies closer to equality than the before-policy curve; Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252.

42743.q: In the graph, the Gini falls and the Lorenz curve moves toward equality. Could a uniform 10% reduction in every household’s income, with nothing else changing, generate that distributional change?
options: Yes; a uniform proportional reduction necessarily moves the Lorenz curve toward equality.
Yes; a uniform proportional reduction eliminates the income gaps measured in percentages.
No; a uniform proportional reduction raises the Gini even though relative shares do not change.
No; a uniform proportional reduction lowers mean income but leaves relative income shares and the Gini unchanged.
42743.feedback: Multiplying every income by 0.9 multiplies each group’s income and the total by the same factor. Shares and relative inequality do not change, so the displayed Gini decline requires a distributional change.
42743.imageAlt: An after-policy Lorenz curve lies closer to equality than the before-policy curve; Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252.

42747.q: Refer to the graph above. Does the graph establish that every low-income household is richer after policy?
options: Yes, because the curve moves up
Yes, because Gini falls
No, because Lorenz curves never compare distributions
No; it shows cumulative relative shares, not each household's income level
42747.feedback: A relative-share improvement does not by itself reveal absolute incomes for every household.

42753.q: At the 40% population point, the graph gives cumulative income of 15%. A student reports a Gini of 0.25 by subtracting 0.15 from 0.40. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The Gini is 0.25 because every pointwise vertical gap equals the entire inequality area.
The 25-percentage-point gap is valid at that point, but Gini depends on the area between the entire Lorenz curve and equality.
The correct Gini is 0.55 because cumulative income and population shares should be added.
The gap is 15 percentage points because the equality line is horizontal at 30%.
42753.feedback: The pointwise gap is 40−15=25 percentage points. It is one height, not the area-based Gini; the rest of the distribution matters.

42761.q: Refer to the graph above. Why is the lower after-policy Gini consistent with the Lorenz curves?
options: The after-policy curve lies farther below equality
The after-policy curve lies closer to the line of equality
The curves must have the same area
The before-policy curve crosses above equality
42761.feedback: A curve closer to the equality line leaves a smaller Gini area, so it is consistent with the lower after-policy coefficient.

ECON-MG-HARD-274.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Before the tax, the equilibrium is $15 and 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and 80 units are sold. What is total tax revenue?
ECON-MG-HARD-274.feedback: The tax is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit. Tax revenue is $6 × 80 = $480.

ECON-MG-HARD-283.q: Refer to the tax graph. What is the per-unit tax, and why is the rise in the buyer price alone insufficient?
options: $6; the buyer price rises $3 and the seller receipt falls $3
$3; only the buyer price change is part of the tax
$18; the entire buyer payment is remitted to government
$33; the original and new buyer prices must be added
ECON-MG-HARD-283.feedback: The taxed quantity is 80. There, buyers pay $18 and sellers receive $12, so the wedge is $6. Relative to the original $15 price, each side bears $3. Using only the buyer increase omits the seller burden.

ECON-MG-HARD-284.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. If students use the original quantity of 100 to calculate tax revenue, what mistake are they making?
options: They are ignoring that the tax reduces quantity sold to 80
They are correctly using the pre-tax market size
They are measuring the buyer burden only
They are calculating a shortage
ECON-MG-HARD-284.feedback: Tax revenue is based on the quantity actually sold after the tax, which is 80 units.

ECON-MG-LEGENDARY-9055.q: Refer to the tax graph. A clerk uses only the buyer price increase as the tax rate and multiplies by the original quantity, reporting $300 of revenue. Which correction addresses both errors?
options: $6 per unit on 80 units gives $480; the report is $180 too low
$3 per unit on 80 units gives $240; the report is $60 too high
$6 per unit on 100 units gives $600; the report is $300 too low
$3 per unit on 100 units gives $300; the report is correct
ECON-MG-LEGENDARY-9055.feedback: The graph gives buyer price $18 and seller receipt $12, so the rate is $6, not the $3 buyer increase. Only 80 units trade after tax. Correct revenue is $480, which exceeds the reported $300 by $180. Fixing only one error still gives the wrong amount.

ECON-MG-LEGENDARY-9057.q: Refer to the tax graph. What happens to market size after the tax is imposed?
options: Quantity falls from 100 to 80 because the tax creates a wedge
Quantity rises from 80 to 100 because the tax raises buyer price
Quantity stays at 100 because tax revenue replaces lost trades
Quantity rises to 150 because sellers receive the old price
ECON-MG-LEGENDARY-9057.feedback: A tax creates a wedge that reduces quantity traded.

ECON-MG-LEGENDARY-9059.q: Refer to the tax graph. Which statement correctly describes the supply + tax curve?
options: It shows sellers require a higher buyer price at each quantity because the tax raises cost per unit
It shows buyers demand more at each price because the tax raises value per unit
It shows the original supply curve shifting right because production is cheaper
It shows the demand curve shifting right because consumers pay the tax
ECON-MG-LEGENDARY-9059.feedback: A seller-side tax shifts supply upward/left by the amount of the tax.

ECON-MG-MEDIUM-186.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What happens to the quantity sold after the tax?
options: It falls from 100 to 80 units
It rises from 80 to 100 units
It stays at 100 units
It rises from 100 to 120 units
ECON-MG-MEDIUM-186.feedback: The tax reduces the quantity sold from 100 units to 80 units.

ECON-MG-MEDIUM-189.q: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Which statement best describes the effect of the tax?
options: The tax creates a wedge and reduces the quantity traded
The tax increases both supply and demand
The tax raises quantity from 80 to 100
The tax removes scarcity from the market
ECON-MG-MEDIUM-189.feedback: The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices and reduces the quantity traded.

P52B-PSIG-EL-001.q: A price rises while quantity sold also rises. Which inference is safest?
options: Demand likely increased, but additional evidence is needed if several forces changed.
Supply must have decreased and nothing else changed.
The higher price caused quantity demanded to rise.
Price signals cannot coordinate markets.
P52B-PSIG-EL-001.commonError: Confusing an equilibrium movement with movement along one curve.
P52B-PSIG-EL-001.feedback: A higher price and quantity are consistent with a demand increase, though simultaneous shifts can complicate diagnosis.

P62B-ELAS-B1-019.q: Checkpoint: At point B, what does the graph imply about total revenue for a small movement in either direction along the same linear demand curve?
options: Total revenue is locally maximized.
Total revenue rises for small movements in both directions.
Total revenue is unchanged at every lower price.
Total revenue is zero at the midpoint.
P62B-ELAS-B1-019.feedback: At B the linear demand curve is unit elastic and revenue is at its local maximum. A small movement in either direction lowers revenue; the first-order change is zero at the exact maximum.

P62B-ELAS-B1-020.q: Checkpoint: Which displayed demand curve has zero price elasticity?
options: D2
D1
Both D1 and D2
Neither D1 nor D2
P62B-ELAS-B1-020.feedback: D2 is vertical, so quantity does not respond to price and elasticity is zero.

P62B-ELAS-B2-019.q: Refer to the graph. Checkpoint: Calculate total revenue at C, B, and A. Which pattern is correct as price falls across those points?
options: Revenue falls through every interval because price falls at each point
Revenue rises in the elastic region, peaks at unit elasticity, then falls in the inelastic region
Revenue stays constant through every interval because the curve has constant slope over the shown interval
Revenue peaks in the inelastic region, then rises as demand becomes more elastic
P62B-ELAS-B2-019.feedback: The total-revenue test tracks the shift from elastic demand above the midpoint to unit elasticity at B and inelastic demand below it.

P62B-ELAS-B2-020.q: Checkpoint: The two supply curves share the same starting point and face the same price increase. Which graph-based reason makes the long-run curve more elastic?
options: Its quantity response is larger
Its price change is larger
Its starting quantity is smaller
Its curve is vertical
P62B-ELAS-B2-020.feedback: With the same price change and starting point, the long-run curve shows the larger percentage quantity response.

P62B-ELAS-B3-008.q: A 10 percent price increase lowers quantity 20 percent. Cost per unit is unchanged. Which revenue-profit statement is safest?
options: Both revenue and profit must rise
Profit must fall by exactly 10 percent
Revenue is unchanged
Revenue falls, but profit direction still requires cost information
P62B-ELAS-B3-008.feedback: Elasticity determines revenue direction, but profit also depends on costs.

P62B-ELAS-B3-020.q: Checkpoint: Using the midpoint formula and the displayed short-run and long-run endpoints, which approximate pair correctly compares supply elasticity?
options: Short run 0.75; long run 0.23
Short run 1.00; long run 1.00
Short run 3.25; long run 0.75
Short run 0.23; long run 0.75
P62B-ELAS-B3-020.feedback: The short-run response is about 0.23 and the long-run response about 0.75, so long-run supply is more elastic.

P62B-ELAS-E-028.q: Refer to the graph. D2 is steeper than D1. Why isn’t slope alone a valid measure of elasticity?
options: Slope and elasticity measure the same response in the same units.
A negative slope makes demand inelastic at every point.
A steeper-looking curve has the same elasticity at every point.
Slope uses units; elasticity compares percentage changes.
P62B-ELAS-E-028.feedback: Slope measures units of price per unit of quantity and changes when axis units change. Elasticity measures percentage responsiveness; classification also depends on the price and quantity being compared.

P62B-ELAS-E-029.q: On the displayed linear demand curve, as you move downward from C through B toward A, price elasticity of demand generally:
options: Declines from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic
Remains constant because slope is constant
Rises from inelastic to elastic
Becomes zero immediately after B
P62B-ELAS-E-029.feedback: C lies in the elastic region, B is the unit-elastic midpoint, and A lies in the inelastic region.

P62B-ELAS-EL-033.q: After calculating total revenue at A, B, and C from the displayed graph, what elasticity condition is associated with the revenue-maximizing point?
options: Demand is unit elastic
Demand is perfectly elastic
Demand is perfectly inelastic
Demand has elasticity greater than 2
P62B-ELAS-EL-033.feedback: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is maximized at the midpoint, where demand is unit elastic.

P62B-ELAS-EL-038.q: Refer to the graph. After a persistent price increase, quantity supplied initially adjusts toward A and, with more time to respond, toward B. Which elasticity principle does this illustrate?
options: Supply tends to become more elastic over longer time horizons
Supply must become perfectly inelastic over time
Short-run supply is always more elastic than long-run supply over the shown interval
Time horizon affects demand but never supply
P62B-ELAS-EL-038.feedback: The larger long-run quantity response illustrates that firms can adjust more fully when given time.

P62B-ELAS-H-016.q: The displayed linear demand curve has constant slope. Why can the upper portion near C be elastic while the lower portion near A is inelastic?
options: The slope changes sign at the midpoint
Consumers become irrational below the midpoint
Price and quantity move in the same direction on the lower portion
Percentage bases differ along the curve despite constant slope
P62B-ELAS-H-016.feedback: Elasticity compares percentage changes, so the price-quantity location matters even when slope is constant.

P62B-ELAS-H-027.q: A cross-price elasticity between ride-share trips and subway rides is 0.2. Which inference is safest?
options: They are strong complements
They are unrelated because 0.2 is below one
They are weak substitutes in the observed range
Both are inferior goods
P62B-ELAS-H-027.feedback: The positive sign indicates substitutes; the small magnitude indicates a weak relationship.

P62B-ELAS-H-028.q: A cross-price elasticity between game consoles and compatible games is −1.4. Which inference is safest?
options: They are substitutes because the magnitude exceeds one
The console is an inferior good
Demand for games is perfectly inelastic
They are relatively strong complements
P62B-ELAS-H-028.feedback: The negative sign indicates complements, and the magnitude suggests a strong link.

P62B-ELAS-H-034.q: Why does elasticity change along the displayed linear demand curve even though the curve has constant slope?
options: The demand curve changes slope at B
The price-to-quantity ratio changes along the curve
Elasticity ignores percentage changes over the shown interval
Quantity becomes fixed below B
P62B-ELAS-H-034.feedback: For a linear demand curve, point elasticity depends on both the constant slope term and the changing P/Q ratio.

P62B-ELAS-L-070.q: A firm estimates a cross-price elasticity of nearly zero between two products. What is the safest conclusion?
options: They are definitively unrelated in every market and period
They are complements because zero is not positive
They are both necessities
Their demands show little observed relationship in the sampled range
P62B-ELAS-L-070.feedback: Near zero indicates weak measured interaction, not an eternal structural claim.

P62B-ELAS-L-091.q: Compare the C→B and B→A intervals on the graph. Why can their elasticity classifications differ?
options: The demand curve has different slopes in the two intervals over the shown interval
The percentage-change bases differ across the two intervals
Elasticity uses only the absolute quantity change
Elasticity is determined only by the direction of price
P62B-ELAS-L-091.feedback: Elasticity depends on percentage changes, so identical absolute changes can produce different elasticities when the average price and quantity bases differ.

P62B-ELAS-L-093.q: Refer to the graph. A seller at C can instead post the price at A or B, but capacity is limited to 70 units and sales equal the smaller of demand and capacity. Which change earns more revenue, and why is demand elasticity alone insufficient?
options: Move to A: revenue is 360; all 90 demanded units can be sold.
Move to A: revenue is 480; a larger price cut guarantees a larger revenue increase.
Stay at C: revenue is 480; capacity makes the B price infeasible.
Move to B: revenue is 480; at A capacity limits revenue to 280.
P62B-ELAS-L-093.feedback: At B, 60 units are demanded and can be sold, earning 8 × 60 = 480. At A, demand is 90 but only 70 can be sold, earning 4 × 70 = 280. C earns 360. Elasticity describes demand, while a binding sales constraint changes realized revenue.

P62B-ELAS-L-095.q: Refer to the graph. Two otherwise comparable products face D1 and D2 over the marked $10-to-$6 interval. Which pairing of substitute availability and revenue response is consistent with midpoint elasticity?
options: D2 plausibly has more close substitutes; the price cut raises D1 revenue but lowers D2 revenue.
D1 plausibly has more close substitutes; the price cut raises D1 revenue but lowers D2 revenue.
D1 plausibly has more close substitutes; the price cut lowers D1 revenue but raises D2 revenue.
Both have the same responsiveness; equal price changes make both revenues unchanged.
P62B-ELAS-L-095.feedback: The midpoint coefficients are about 1.43 for D1 and 0.89 for D2. More substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness, not proof from slope alone. Revenue changes from 450 to 570 on D1 and from 350 to 330 on D2.

P62B-ELAS-M-008.q: Refer to the graph. As you move down the linear demand curve from C through B toward A, price elasticity of demand generally:
options: Increase
Decline
Remain constant
Switch immediately from zero to infinity
P62B-ELAS-M-008.feedback: The price-to-quantity ratio falls as movement continues down the line, so elasticity declines.

P62B-ELAS-M-028.q: The displayed linear demand curve has constant slope, yet elasticity changes along it. Which statement correctly compares slope and elasticity?
options: Slope and elasticity are both constant everywhere on a linear demand curve
Slope is constant on a linear demand curve, but elasticity usually changes along it
Elasticity is constant on a linear demand curve, but slope usually changes along it
Slope and elasticity both change only when a demand curve is nonlinear
P62B-ELAS-M-028.feedback: Elasticity also depends on the price and quantity at the point.

P62B-ELAS-M-037.q: Refer to the graph. As price changes between the two labeled points on vertical D2, what happens to quantity demanded?
options: It remains 50 units
It rises to 70 units
It falls to 30 units
It becomes zero
P62B-ELAS-M-037.feedback: D2 is vertical at Q = 50, so the price change does not alter quantity demanded.

P62B-ELAS-M-039.q: Refer to the graph. Compare the short-run and long-run supply responses to the same price change. Why is the long-run response larger?
options: Producers have less time to change output over the shown interval
Producers have more time to adjust capacity and inputs
Long-run quantity is fixed by definition
Price changes are smaller in the long run
P62B-ELAS-M-039.feedback: More adjustment time usually allows firms to expand capacity, enter, switch inputs, and otherwise respond more strongly.

P62C-CPS-B2-007.q: Use the graph with demand intercept $30 and equilibrium E at Q=8, P=$14. A student labels the $112 revenue rectangle as consumer surplus. Which correction is right?
options: Consumer surplus is the $64 triangle above price and below demand; $112 is expenditure transferred to sellers.
Consumer surplus is $112 because every dollar paid is a buyer gain.
Consumer surplus is $32 because the supply intercept determines the buyer triangle.
Consumer surplus is $176 because add the demand triangle to all payments.
P62C-CPS-B2-007.feedback: The buyer triangle is 0.5×8×(30−14)=$64. The rectangle 8×14=$112 is payment for the goods, not the buyer’s net gain.

P62C-CPS-B2-008.q: Use the graph with supply intercept $6 and E at Q=8, P=$14. A lump-sum rule transfers $20 from buyers to sellers without changing quantity, allocation or resource costs. What is producer surplus after the transfer, and what happens to total surplus?
options: Producer surplus rises from $32 to $52; total surplus is unchanged.
Producer surplus rises from $32 to $52; total surplus rises $20.
Producer surplus falls from $32 to $12; total surplus is unchanged.
Producer surplus starts at $112 and rises to $132; total surplus rises $20.
P62C-CPS-B2-008.feedback: Initial producer surplus is 0.5×8×(14−6)=$32. The $20 transfer raises sellers’ share to $52 and lowers buyers’ share by the same amount, leaving total surplus unchanged.

P62C-CPS-B2-009.q: In the graph, demand intercepts price at $30, supply at $6 and E is Q=8, P=$14. A report adds the $112 sales revenue to consumer and producer surplus when measuring gains from exchange. What is the correct total and diagnosis?
options: Total surplus is $96; adding revenue double-counts a payment already separating buyer and seller shares.
Total surplus is $208; revenue is an additional benefit beyond consumer and producer surplus.
Total surplus is $112; payments alone measure the gains from exchange.
Total surplus is $64; producer gains should be excluded because sellers receive payments.
P62C-CPS-B2-009.feedback: CS=0.5×8×16=$64 and PS=0.5×8×8=$32, totaling $96. Revenue is a transfer from buyers to sellers, not an extra resource benefit.

P62C-CPS-B2-010.q: In the compact graph, straight demand runs from P=$24 to E at Q=5, P=$14; straight supply runs from P=$4 to E. A quota stops production at Q=4, allocating the units efficiently. How much surplus is forgone on the missing output between 4 and 5?
options: $2: at Q=4 demand is $16 and supply $12, so the missing triangle is 0.5×1×4.
$4: multiply the one-unit base by the full $4 height without halving.
$14: every missing unit loses its market price as surplus.
$10: subtract the equilibrium price from the demand intercept without using quantity.
P62C-CPS-B2-010.feedback: Demand is 24−2Q and supply 4+2Q. Their gap at Q=4 is 16−12=$4 and reaches zero at Q=5. The forgone triangle is $2.

P62C-CPS-EL-017.q: Refer to the graph. Why is producer surplus zero even though firms receive revenue?
options: Price equals marginal cost on every traded unit
Demand slopes downward
Quantity is positive
Consumer surplus absorbs revenue
P62C-CPS-EL-017.feedback: Every unit has cost equal to price.

P62C-CPS-H-005.q: Refer to the balanced-market graph. Which amount and region represent consumer surplus at E?
options: $32, below demand and above the market price, up to the traded quantity
$32, above supply and below the market price, up to the traded quantity
$80, the price-times-quantity rectangle
$64, the entire region between demand and supply up to E
P62C-CPS-H-005.feedback: At E, quantity is 8 and price is $10. Consumer surplus is 0.5 × 8 × ($18 − $10) = $32. The equally sized area above supply is producer surplus; expenditure is $80 and total surplus is $64.

P62C-CPS-H-007.q: Refer to the graph. At E, what is total surplus, and why is it different from buyer expenditure?
options: $50; it measures value above production cost, rather than payments
$70; it equals the price paid for all units
$25; it includes only the area above the price
$100; it is the full intercept-gap rectangle
P62C-CPS-H-007.feedback: The graph gives Q = 5, P = $14, demand intercept $24 and supply intercept $4. CS and PS are each $25, so total surplus is $50. Payments of $70 transfer money between market participants.

P62C-CPS-L-002.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [28, 34, 40, 46, 52]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [45, 37, 53, 41, 49]. Values and costs are in dollars. Exactly 2 units are produced by the cheapest sellers, but the lowest-valued buyer receives one instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 2 values. What would reallocating that one unit, with no transaction cost, do?
options: Leave total surplus unchanged because output does not change.
Raise total surplus by $18 without changing output.
Lower total surplus by $18 because the original recipient loses the item.
Raise total surplus by $46 because the replaced buyer’s value is irrelevant.
P62C-CPS-L-002.feedback: The relevant buyer-value difference is $46−$28=$18. Production costs and quantity stay fixed, so that increase in use value is the change in total surplus.

P62C-CPS-L-007.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [54, 48, 42, 36, 30]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [39, 43, 47, 51, 55]. Values and costs are in dollars. Exactly 2 units are produced by the cheapest sellers, but the lowest-valued buyer receives one instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 2 values. What would reallocating that one unit, with no transaction cost, do?
options: Leave total surplus unchanged because output does not change.
Lower total surplus by $18 because the original recipient loses the item.
Raise total surplus by $18 without changing output.
Raise total surplus by $48 because the replaced buyer’s value is irrelevant.
P62C-CPS-L-007.feedback: The relevant buyer-value difference is $48−$30=$18. Production costs and quantity stay fixed, so that increase in use value is the change in total surplus.

P62C-CPS-L-012.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [32, 38, 44, 50, 56]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [49, 41, 57, 45, 53]. Values and costs are in dollars. Exactly 2 units are produced by the cheapest sellers, but the lowest-valued buyer receives one instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 2 values. What would reallocating that one unit, with no transaction cost, do?
options: Leave total surplus unchanged because output does not change.
Lower total surplus by $18 because the original recipient loses the item.
Raise total surplus by $50 because the replaced buyer’s value is irrelevant.
Raise total surplus by $18 without changing output.
P62C-CPS-L-012.feedback: The relevant buyer-value difference is $50−$32=$18. Production costs and quantity stay fixed, so that increase in use value is the change in total surplus.

P62C-CPS-L-020.q: In the balanced market graph, why is Q = 8 the efficient quantity under the standard competitive assumptions?
options: Consumer and producer surplus must be numerically equal there
Every buyer and seller earns positive surplus there
The market price is the fairest possible price there
The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal seller’s cost there
P62C-CPS-L-020.feedback: At the efficient quantity, marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost. Equality of consumer and producer surplus is not required.

P62C-CPS-L-024.q: Why is the quantity at E efficient in the asymmetric graph under the standard competitive assumptions?
options: Consumer and producer surplus must be numerically equal there
Every buyer and seller earns positive surplus there
The market price is the fairest possible price there
The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal seller’s cost there
P62C-CPS-L-024.feedback: At the efficient quantity, marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost. Equality of consumer and producer surplus is not required.

P62C-CPS-L-028.q: In the graph, why is Q = 5 the efficient quantity under the standard competitive assumptions?
options: Consumer and producer surplus must be numerically equal there
Every buyer and seller earns positive surplus there
The market price is the fairest possible price there
The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal seller’s cost there
P62C-CPS-L-028.feedback: At the efficient quantity, marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost. Equality of consumer and producer surplus is not required.

P62C-CPS-L-029.q: The underproduction graph shows output at Q = 6 although the competitive quantity is Q = 8. What is the decisive evidence that output should expand?
options: At Q = 6, marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost
At Q = 6, consumer surplus equals producer surplus
At Q = 6, price must be below every seller’s cost
At Q = 6, all possible gains from exchange have already occurred
P62C-CPS-L-029.feedback: When marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost, the next units create positive gains from exchange.

P62C-CPS-L-030.q: Refer to the underproduction graph. A rule holds output at the marked quantity left of E. Repealing it restores E but also transfers $9 from producers to consumers on units still traded. What is the total-surplus change, assuming efficient allocation and no other effects?
options: A $13 increase; add the transfer to the recovered gains
A $4 increase; the $9 changes distribution
A $5 decrease; the transfer costs more than the recovered gains
A $9 increase; only the transfer changes welfare
P62C-CPS-L-030.feedback: The omitted triangle has width 8 − 6 = 2 and height 12 − 8 = $4, so restored gains are $4. The $9 transfer adds to CS and subtracts from PS equally. It does not change combined surplus.

P62C-CPS-L-031.q: The overproduction graph shows output at Q = 10 although the competitive quantity is Q = 8. Why do the last two units reduce total surplus?

Marginal cost
Average variable cost
Economic profit

TP falls and MP is negative

AP should rise
AP must become zero
AP must turn negative

TP rises while AP falls
TP is constant while AP rises

options: MC and AVC rise; the firm’s quantity supplied falls at a given price
AFC alone rises; MC is unchanged; current output is unchanged
MC and AVC fall; the firm’s quantity supplied rises at a given price
ATC alone rises; the firm independently changes the market price
P62F-PC-L-041.feedback: Classify the change as fixed, variable, or productivity-related before applying the output and shutdown rules.

P62F-PC-L-042.q: Piece-rate compensation per completed unit increases. Which combined curve-and-decision result is correct?
options: AFC alone rises; MC is unchanged; current output is unchanged
MC and AVC rise; the firm’s quantity supplied falls at a given price
MC and AVC fall; the firm’s quantity supplied rises at a given price
ATC alone rises; the firm independently changes the market price
P62F-PC-L-042.feedback: Classify the change as fixed, variable, or productivity-related before applying the output and shutdown rules.

P62F-PC-L-043.q: A lump-sum operating subsidy is paid regardless of current output. Which combined curve-and-decision result is correct?
options: MC and AVC fall; current output rises at the given price
AFC and ATC rise; MC is unchanged; current output is unchanged
AFC and ATC fall; MC and AVC are unchanged; current output is unchanged
AFC alone falls; ATC is unchanged; the firm changes its price
P62F-PC-L-043.feedback: Classify the change as fixed, variable, or productivity-related before applying the output and shutdown rules.

P62F-PC-L-044.q: An annual grant covers part of the plant lease but does not depend on quantity. Which combined curve-and-decision result is correct?
options: MC and AVC fall; current output rises at the given price
AFC and ATC rise; MC is unchanged; current output is unchanged
AFC alone falls; ATC is unchanged; the firm changes its price
AFC and ATC fall; MC and AVC are unchanged; current output is unchanged
P62F-PC-L-044.feedback: Classify the change as fixed, variable, or productivity-related before applying the output and shutdown rules.

P62F-PC-L-045.q: A one-time rebate reduces unavoidable annual overhead. Which combined curve-and-decision result is correct?
options: AFC and ATC fall; MC and AVC are unchanged; current output is unchanged
MC and AVC fall; current output rises at the given price
AFC and ATC rise; MC is unchanged; current output is unchanged
AFC alone falls; ATC is unchanged; the firm changes its price
P62F-PC-L-045.feedback: Classify the change as fixed, variable, or productivity-related before applying the output and shutdown rules.

P62F-PC-L-061.q: Refer to the graph. What is the correct order for analyzing the firm’s output and economic profit?
options: Use P=MC on rising MC to find Q1, then measure P−ATC at Q1
Choose the minimum ATC output first
Use market quantity as firm output
Measure profit before selecting output
P62F-PC-L-061.feedback: The horizontal price line is also MR. Its intersection with rising MC selects Q1; only then can the price–ATC gap at Q1 establish per-unit profit.

P62F-PC-L-062.q: Refer to the graph. What does the vertical gap between the price line and ATC at Q1 measure?
options: Total economic profit
Economic profit per unit
Producer surplus for the whole market
Marginal revenue minus marginal cost at every output
P62F-PC-L-062.feedback: Price and ATC are both dollars per unit, so their vertical difference is economic profit per unit. Multiplying that gap by Q1 would give total profit.

P62F-PC-L-063.q: Refer to the graph. The price line touches minimum ATC at the selected output. What follows?
options: The firm must exit
Accounting profit must be zero
The firm earns zero economic profit while covering normal profit
The firm is below shutdown price
P62F-PC-L-063.feedback: At the selected output P=ATC, so total revenue equals total economic cost. Implicit owner returns are included in that cost, making zero economic profit compatible with normal profit.

P62F-PC-L-064.q: Refer to the graph. Price lies below ATC but above AVC at the rising-MC output. What is the short-run decision?
options: Shut down and eliminate fixed cost
Produce at minimum ATC instead
Raise price to ATC
Produce and incur an economic loss
P62F-PC-L-064.feedback: P above AVC means production covers variable cost and contributes toward unavoidable fixed cost. P below ATC means that contribution does not cover all fixed cost, so operating still incurs an economic loss.

P62F-PC-L-065.q: Refer to the loss-making firm graph. Assume all firms are initially identical, fixed costs cannot be avoided this period, and input prices and cost curves stay unchanged as firms leave. Which sequence correctly separates present operation from eventual adjustment?
options: The firm operates because P exceeds AVC; persistent losses induce exit; market supply falls and survivors’ MR and output rise until losses disappear
The firm shuts down solely because P is below ATC; shutdown immediately removes all fixed costs and eliminates losses
Losses induce entry; market supply rises and each survivor’s horizontal MR rises until zero profit
Survivors raise their own selling prices first; their downward-sloping demand curves then shift right
P62F-PC-L-065.feedback: The displayed price lies between AVC and ATC, so production covers variable cost and some unavoidable fixed cost. Persistent economic losses discourage renewal and induce exit. Reduced market supply raises price and each survivor’s horizontal MR; output rises along unchanged rising MC until the standard long-run zero-profit condition is restored.

P62F-PC-L-066.q: Refer to the graph. Price is below minimum AVC. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The firm produces where price meets MC
The firm supplies zero in the short run and bears fixed cost
The firm breaks even
The firm raises the market price
P62F-PC-L-066.feedback: Price below minimum AVC cannot cover variable cost at any positive output. Shutdown avoids variable cost but leaves unavoidable short-run fixed cost.

P62F-PC-L-067.q: Refer to the graph. Which segment traces the price-taking firm’s short-run supply?
options: The entire MC curve
The AVC curve
The rising MC segment at and above minimum AVC
The falling portion of MC below AVC
P62F-PC-L-067.feedback: Above minimum AVC, each price selects the quantity where the rising MC curve equals that price. Below the shutdown threshold the firm supplies zero, so the entire MC curve is not supply.

P62F-PC-L-068.q: Refer to the graph. How should information move from the market panel to the firm panel?
options: The firm panel determines market price
Market quantity becomes firm quantity
The firm chooses P1 and the market chooses its output
Market supply and demand determine P1; the firm uses P1 as MR to choose its own quantity
P62F-PC-L-068.feedback: The market panel determines P1 from market supply and demand. The individual price taker faces that price as a horizontal MR line and uses its own MC to select firm output, not market quantity.

P62F-PC-L-069.q: Refer to the graph. The initial firm price produces economic profit. What explains the market-supply shift shown?
options: Entry by firms attracted by the profit
Exit by loss-making firms
A single firm cutting price
A fall in market demand
P62F-PC-L-069.feedback: Economic profit attracts entrants, adding output at each market price. The rightward supply shift lowers price and erodes incumbent profit.

P62F-PC-L-070.q: Refer to the graph. The initial firm price produces an economic loss. What explains the market-supply shift shown?
options: Entry expands supply and raises the survivors’ market price
Exit reduces supply and raises the survivors’ market price
Exit expands supply and lowers the survivors’ market price
Entry reduces supply and lowers the survivors’ market price
P62F-PC-L-070.feedback: Economic losses induce exit over time. Fewer firms shift market supply left; with demand fixed, price rises for surviving firms and their losses diminish.

P62F-PC-L-071.q: Refer to the graph. What does the horizontal long-run industry supply curve imply?
options: Each firm has horizontal MC
Demand is perfectly elastic for the market
Industry expansion does not change firms’ minimum long-run average cost
Economic profit remains positive
P62F-PC-L-071.feedback: A horizontal long-run industry supply means additional industry output can be produced at the same minimum unit cost. It does not imply each individual firm has horizontal MC.

P62F-PC-L-072.q: Refer to the graph. Why does this long-run industry supply curve slope upward?
options: Individual firms set higher prices
Marginal revenue slopes upward
Entry permanently increases economic profit
Industry expansion raises input costs or other firm costs
P62F-PC-L-072.feedback: Expansion bids up inputs or otherwise raises firms’ costs. The higher long-run break-even cost requires a higher price to support the larger industry output.

P62F-PC-L-073.q: Refer to the graph. What can produce the downward-sloping long-run industry supply shown?
options: External economies that lower firm costs as the industry expands
Rising input prices
A downward-sloping individual firm demand curve
A shutdown price above ATC
P62F-PC-L-073.feedback: External economies from industry expansion lower firms’ costs, permitting a lower break-even price at a larger industry output. Rising input prices would have the opposite effect.

P62F-PC-L-074.q: Refer to the graph. At the long-run benchmark, which two conditions hold?
options: P=AVC and economic profit is positive
P=MC and P=minimum ATC
P>MC and P>ATC
MC is below AVC
P62F-PC-L-074.feedback: At the depicted benchmark P=MC matches marginal value with marginal cost, while P=minimum ATC covers total economic cost at its minimum. These establish allocative and productive efficiency respectively.

P62F-PC-L-075.q: Refer to the graph. For the increasing-cost industry shown, how does the new long-run price compare with the original after demand rises?
options: It returns exactly to the original price
It falls below the original price
It remains above the original price but below the short-run peak
It remains at the short-run peak forever
P62F-PC-L-075.feedback: Higher demand first raises price and creates profit. Entry then expands supply and lowers price from that peak, but industry expansion raises input costs, so the new long-run break-even price remains above the original.

P62F-PC-L-091.q: Refer to the graph. Which sequence correctly extracts the firm’s economic profit from the graph?
options: Choose minimum ATC first; multiply that output by the $30 market price to obtain economic profit
Use AVC = $10 as profit per unit; multiply $10 by Q = 50 to obtain total profit
Use rising-MC P = MC to get Q = 50; read ATC = $20; compute ($30 − $20) × 50
Use market price $30 as profit per unit; multiply it by Q = 50 without subtracting cost
P62F-PC-L-091.feedback: Competitive-firm analysis chooses Q from P = MC first, then measures P − ATC at that quantity.

P62F-PC-L-092.q: Refer to the graph. At the selected output, compare price with ATC. Which statement about economic profit is most accurate?
options: The firm necessarily earns zero accounting profit because economic and accounting costs are identical
The firm should shut down because any zero-profit outcome fails to cover average variable cost
The firm bears a loss equal to total fixed cost because price only covers its variable cost
The firm earns zero economic profit while covering the normal return included in economic cost
P62F-PC-L-092.feedback: Economic cost includes opportunity cost, so zero economic profit is consistent with normal profit.

P62F-PC-L-093.q: Refer to the graph. If market price fell slightly below $25 but remained above AVC, with the cost curves unchanged, what would the firm do in the short run?
options: Choose the lower-price rising-MC intersection and operate with a loss as long as price remains above AVC
Shut down immediately because any price below ATC makes short-run production economically irrational for the displayed firm
Keep Q fixed at 50 because price-taking firms never change output when the market price changes
Raise the firm’s own price back to $25 and continue producing at the original break-even output
P62F-PC-L-093.feedback: A competitive firm continues producing when price covers AVC, even if price is below ATC.

P62F-PC-L-094.q: Refer to the graph. Trace the firm’s short-run and long-run logic in the loss case. Which sequence is valid?
options: Choose Q = 30 where P = MC; because AVC < P < ATC, operate with a $300 loss and face exit pressure if it persists
Choose minimum ATC; because P equals ATC there, operate with zero profit and no exit pressure for the displayed firm
Shut down at Q = 0; because P < ATC, avoid all variable and fixed costs immediately
Raise price to $40; keep Q = 30 and convert the displayed loss into economic profit
P62F-PC-L-094.feedback: The firm covers variable cost but not total cost, so it operates in the short run and may exit in the long run.

P62F-PC-L-095.q: Refer to the graph. The $10 price line can intersect MC at a low-output portion of the curve. Why is that intersection not the firm’s chosen output?
options: The firm must always choose the highest feasible output, so any low-output MC crossing is irrelevant
ATC must fall to zero before a firm can produce, so the low-output crossing cannot be used
A competitive firm ignores marginal cost at low output and chooses quantity from average total cost instead
P is below minimum AVC, so the shutdown condition rules out the low-output P = MC crossing
P62F-PC-L-095.feedback: P = MC is not sufficient; the chosen point must also satisfy the shutdown condition and lie on rising MC.

P62F-PC-L-096.q: Refer to the graph. If price were exactly $20 at point A, which statement would be correct?
options: The firm is indifferent between producing at the shutdown output and shutting down in the short run
The firm earns positive economic profit because price equals the minimum of average variable cost for the displayed firm
The firm must exit immediately because reaching minimum AVC makes long-run production impossible
The firm instead produces at point C because ATC determines the short-run shutdown quantity
P62F-PC-L-096.feedback: At minimum AVC, revenue exactly covers variable cost, making the firm indifferent in the short run.

P62F-PC-L-097.q: Refer to the graph. Which chain correctly describes the adjustment implied by the two panels?
options: Market sets P = $40; firm chooses Q = 90; profit attracts entry; supply rises; price and firm output fall
Firm chooses P = $40; market adopts Q = 90; losses cause exit; supply rises and price falls
Market sets Q = 90 for every firm; entry occurs but leaves both market price and firm output unchanged for the displayed firm
Firm chooses minimum AVC; entry shifts market demand right and raises both price and individual output
P62F-PC-L-097.feedback: The market determines price, the firm chooses output, and persistent profit triggers entry and lower price.

P62F-PC-L-099.q: Refer to the graph. Trace the paired market-and-firm loss case through long-run adjustment. Which sequence is valid?
options: Market sets P = $15; firm shuts down because P < ATC; persistent shutdown attracts entry and lowers price for the displayed firm
Firm sets P = $15; market adopts Q = 50; persistent profit causes entry and higher market supply
Market sets firm ATC at $18; firm shifts market demand left until price equals average cost
Market sets P = $15; firm chooses Q = 50; AVC < P < ATC creates a loss; persistent loss causes exit and higher price
P62F-PC-L-099.feedback: The firm operates in the short run because P > AVC, but persistent loss creates exit pressure.

P62F-PC-LB-013.q: Use the market and representative-firm panels. An analyst assigns the market’s total quantity to each firm and recommends producing at minimum ATC whenever that differs from the MR=MC quantity. Which correction preserves both the market-firm distinction and the operating decision?
options: Divide market price by the number of firms, assign market quantity to each firm, and use ATC alone to decide shutdown.
Take price from the market, but choose minimum ATC before considering MR; firms can then sell any desired amount at that cost.
Take price from the market, choose each operating firm’s output on rising MC at that price, and check AVC before production and ATC for profit.
Take the firm’s MC as the market demand curve, choose market quantity there, and ignore AVC if revenue is positive.
P62F-PC-LB-013.feedback: Market quantity is the sum of firms’ outputs, not the output of each firm. A price taker has MR=P; the candidate output satisfies rising MC=P when operating. AVC governs shutdown, while ATC determines economic profit.

P62F-PC-LB-015.q: The graph initially shows P above ATC at Q1. An unavoidable fee for the current year raises fixed cost by more than the initial total profit, leaving demand, MC and AVC unchanged. The fee is avoidable by leaving before next year. Which sequence is correct?
options: Keep the same short-run output but incur a loss; if these conditions persist, exit can avoid the future fee.
Reduce short-run output because the fee raises MC; continue permanently because P still covers AVC.
Keep the same short-run output and profit because a fixed fee never affects profit.
Shut down immediately and avoid this year’s fee; reenter next year if P remains above AVC.
P62F-PC-LB-015.feedback: The fee does not change the MR=MC output or the current operating margin over variable cost. It does reduce profit, possibly below zero. A fee unavoidable now but avoidable next year separates short-run operation from long-run exit.

P62F-PC-LB-016.q: The graph shows AVC<P<ATC at the operating quantity Q1. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. A student says shutting down removes the entire loss (ATC−P)Q1. Which comparison correctly evaluates production versus shutdown?
options: Producing incurs (ATC−P)Q1, while shutdown loses zero because all costs become avoidable immediately.
Producing incurs (ATC−P)Q1, while shutdown loses all fixed cost; producing covers (P−AVC)Q1 of that fixed cost and is preferable now.
Producing covers no fixed cost because P<ATC, so shutdown and production necessarily have identical losses.
Producing earns positive economic profit because P>AVC, so the stated loss rectangle should be ignored.
P62F-PC-LB-016.feedback: Revenue exceeds variable cost, so production contributes a positive amount toward unavoidable fixed cost. The operating loss is smaller than the fixed-cost loss under shutdown, although persistent losses can still lead to long-run exit.

P62F-PC-LB-017.q: The graph shows a firm below its AVC shutdown threshold. Compare an unconditional lump-sum grant with a per-unit subsidy large enough to raise the firm’s net receipt above that threshold. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. Which operating comparison is correct?
options: Both policies change marginal receipts equally, so either grant necessarily restores production.
The lump-sum grant lowers MC and restores production, while the per-unit subsidy affects fixed cost only.
The lump-sum grant alone leaves the shutdown decision unchanged; the per-unit subsidy changes marginal receipts and can make production worthwhile.
Neither policy can change production because any firm with an initial loss must shut down forever.
P62F-PC-LB-017.feedback: An unconditional grant does not change the payoff difference between producing and not producing. A per-unit subsidy is earned only on output and changes the net price compared with MC and AVC, potentially crossing the operating threshold.

P62F-PC-LB-018.q: Use the short-run supply graph. Compare a rise in unavoidable fixed rent with a rise in the variable cost of every unit produced, holding market demand unchanged. Which statement separates the two effects on firm supply?
options: Both costs shift short-run supply upward by the same amount because both increase ATC.
The fixed rent shifts short-run supply upward, while higher variable cost affects only long-run exit.
Neither cost affects supply until entry occurs because a price-taking firm cannot change output.
The fixed rent alone leaves MC and AVC, and thus short-run supply, unchanged; higher variable cost can raise MC and the shutdown threshold.
P62F-PC-LB-018.feedback: The operating supply relation uses rising MC above minimum AVC. Fixed rent does not enter either marginal or variable cost, although it affects profit and later exit. Variable-cost changes directly affect the operating comparison.

P62F-PC-M-032.q: Refer to the graph. At the 50-unit output, what vertical price–ATC gap represents profit on each unit?
options: $10 per unit
$20 per unit
$30 per unit
$40 per unit
P62F-PC-M-032.feedback: Profit per unit is P − ATC = $30 − $20 = $10.

P62F-PC-M-036.q: Refer to the graph. The blue ATC guide at the chosen 30-unit output lands on which dollar value?
P62F-PC-M-036.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 30 is $40.

P62F-PC-M-037.q: Refer to the graph. The green AVC marker at Q = 30 gives what variable cost per unit?
P62F-PC-M-037.feedback: The AVC guide at Q = 30 is $20.

P62F-PC-M-040.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the firm’s short-run supply curve begin?
options: At the left end of the entire MC curve
At point C and then along ATC
At point A and then along rising MC
Along the AVC curve below A
P62F-PC-M-040.feedback: Short-run supply is rising MC at and above minimum AVC.

P62F-PC-M-041.q: Refer to the graph. At the 90-unit output in the paired profit graph, what vertical price–ATC gap represents profit per unit?
options: $20 per unit
$5 per unit
$15 per unit
$40 per unit
P62F-PC-M-041.feedback: Price is $40 and ATC is $20, so profit per unit is $20.

P62F-PC-M-043.q: Refer to the graph. How does the market-panel equilibrium price enter the representative firm’s decision?
options: It becomes the firm’s ATC curve, determining average cost at every possible output level
It becomes the firm’s quantity of 75, so market quantity and individual output are identical
It becomes the firm’s horizontal P = MR = AR line used to choose output along MC
It shifts the firm’s MC curve upward, changing production cost without changing marginal revenue
P62F-PC-M-043.feedback: A price-taking firm accepts the market price as its marginal and average revenue.

P62F-PC-M-046.q: Refer to the graph. Use price and AVC at the chosen output. Why does the representative firm continue producing in the short run?
options: P = $15 exceeds AVC = $10 at Q = 50, so revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost
P = $15 exceeds ATC = $18 at Q = 50, so the firm is earning positive economic profit
The competitive firm can raise its own price above $15, so it avoids the loss shown by ATC
Producing at Q = 50 eliminates fixed cost, so any price above AVC guarantees zero economic loss
P62F-PC-M-046.feedback: The firm covers variable cost and part of fixed cost because P > AVC.

P62F-PC-M-047.q: Refer to the graph. What economic profit does the representative firm earn at the long-run equilibrium?
P62F-PC-M-047.feedback: Price equals ATC at the selected output, so economic profit is zero.

P62F-PC-M-048.q: Refer to the graph. Which pair of conditions holds at the representative firm’s selected output?
options: P < AVC and MC < ATC for the displayed firm
P = MC and P = minimum ATC
P > ATC and MC < AVC
P = AVC and ATC = 0
P62F-PC-M-048.feedback: Long-run competitive equilibrium has P = MC and P at minimum ATC.

P62G-MON-B2-020.q: At Granite Utility’s optimum, P=$61.90, ATC=$35.03, AVC=$21.90, and Q=19.05. Which comparison controls shutdown?

Price compared with AVC
MR compared with demand
Fixed cost compared with total revenue

P62G-MON-B3-057.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison best captures the unregulated monopoly outcome and the allocatively efficient outcome?
options: Unregulated: Q = 90, P = $20; efficient: Q = 45, P = $47
Unregulated: Q = 45, P = $47; efficient D = MC: Q = 90, P = $20
Unregulated: Q = 45, P = $20; efficient: Q = 90, P = $47
Both outcomes occur at Q = 45 because MC is horizontal
P62G-MON-B3-057.feedback: MR = MC determines the unregulated monopoly output, while D = MC identifies the allocatively efficient benchmark.

P62G-MON-B3-058.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly contrasts fair-return pricing with marginal-cost pricing?
options: Fair-return sets P = MC at Q = 140; MC pricing sets P = ATC near Q = 116
Both rules preserve the unregulated price near $27 and leave output close to Q = 70
MC pricing produces less output than fair-return pricing because the MC curve is horizontal
Fair-return covers ATC near Q = 116; MC pricing reaches Q = 140 but P < ATC
P62G-MON-B3-058.feedback: The graph shows the classic tradeoff: average-cost pricing supports break-even, while marginal-cost pricing reaches the efficient quantity but may require a subsidy.

P62G-MON-EL-031.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose fixed cost rises by $360 while demand, MR, and MC remain unchanged. What happens to the monopoly choice and economic profit?
options: Q and P stay at 36 and $42; profit falls from $540 to $180
Q falls to 24 and P rises to $48; profit stays $540
Q rises to 60 and P falls to $30; profit becomes zero
Q and P stay at 36 and $42; profit rises to $900
P62G-MON-EL-031.feedback: A fixed-cost change does not alter MR or MC, so Q and P stay put. Profit falls dollar-for-dollar by $360.

P62G-MON-EL-032.q: Refer to the graph. Why would moving output from 36 toward the D = MC quantity of 60 reduce allocative inefficiency?
options: MR exceeds price on every unit through Q = 60
Demand exceeds MC on the additional units
ATC is constant between Q = 36 and Q = 60
The monopoly price stays fixed at $42 as output expands
P62G-MON-EL-032.feedback: Between the monopoly quantity and D = MC, demand lies above MC, so mutually beneficial units are not produced under monopoly.

P62G-MON-EL-033.q: Refer to the graph. If ATC at Q = 40 fell from $45 to $35 while demand, MR, and MC remained unchanged, what would result?
options: The firm switches to Q = 67 and earns zero economic profit
Price falls automatically from $40 to the new ATC of $35
Q = 40 and P = $40 stay; the firm still loses $200
Q = 40 and P = $40 stay; profit becomes $200
P62G-MON-EL-033.feedback: The marginal decision is unchanged. Profit becomes ($40 − $35) × 40 = $200.

P62G-MON-EL-034.q: Refer to the graph. What feature shows the allocative gap created by monopoly?
options: Demand stays above MC between Q = 40 and Q ≈ 67
MR stays above demand between Q = 40 and Q ≈ 67
ATC stays below price at the monopoly quantity of 40
MC is horizontal between the monopoly and benchmark outputs
P62G-MON-EL-034.feedback: Units between the monopoly quantity and D = MC have marginal benefit above marginal cost but are not produced.

P62G-MON-EL-036.q: Refer to the graph. Why can marginal-cost pricing create a financing problem for this natural monopoly?
options: At Q = 90, MR is above the demand price
At Q = 45, price is below marginal cost
At Q = 90, ATC is above the $20 regulated price
ATC rises sharply as output expands from 45 to 90
P62G-MON-EL-036.feedback: With economies of scale, ATC can exceed MC at the efficient output, so P = MC may not cover total cost.

P62G-MON-EL-037.q: Refer to the graph. Compared with the unregulated monopoly outcome, moving to D = MC would:
options: Halve output from 90 to 45 and raise price from $20 to $47
Keep output at 45 while cutting price to $20
Raise output to 125 while leaving price at $47
Double output from 45 to 90 and cut price from $47 to $20
P62G-MON-EL-037.feedback: The marked outcomes are Q = 45, P = $47 for monopoly and Q = 90, P = $20 at D = MC.

P62G-MON-EL-038.q: Refer to the graph. Which price-output ordering is consistent with the outcomes shown?
options: Prices rise $10 → $16 → $27 as output rises 70 → 116 → 140
Price stays $27 while output rises 70 → 140
Prices fall $27 → $16 → $10 as output rises 70 → 116 → 140
Output falls 140 → 70 as prices fall $27 → $10
P62G-MON-EL-038.feedback: Stronger regulation toward marginal-cost pricing lowers price and expands output in the displayed natural monopoly.

P62G-MON-EL-039.q: Refer to the graph. Why is average-cost pricing less allocatively efficient than marginal-cost pricing?
options: Fair-return leaves P < MC and Q above 140 units
Average-cost pricing reaches D = MC and produces positive profit
Average-cost pricing makes demand horizontal at the regulated price
Fair-return leaves P > MC and Q below 140 units
P62G-MON-EL-039.feedback: Fair-return pricing covers costs but stops short of the D = MC quantity because P remains above MC.

P62G-MON-EL-040.q: Refer to the graph. Why might the regulator need a subsidy under marginal-cost pricing?
options: P = $10 is below ATC = $15 at Q = 140
P = $27 exceeds ATC at Q = 70
P = $16 equals ATC at Q = 116
MR is greater than demand at Q = 140
P62G-MON-EL-040.feedback: At the efficient quantity, total revenue at P = MC does not cover average total cost.

P62G-MON-H-002.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison determines whether the monopolist earns economic profit at Q1?
options: P1 compared with MC at Q1
P1 compared with ATC at Q1
MR compared with demand at Q1
ATC compared with AVC at zero output

P62G-MON-H-003.q: Refer to the graph. At Q1, why is price greater than marginal revenue?
options: Marginal cost includes fixed cost
Demand is perfectly elastic
Lowering price to sell Q1 creates a price effect on prior units
Average revenue is below demand
P62G-MON-H-003.feedback: For single-price monopoly, MR reflects both the output and price effects.

P62G-MON-H-004.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose fixed cost rises while demand, MR, and MC remain unchanged. What happens in the short run?
options: Q1 falls and P1 rises
Q1 rises and P1 falls
The MR curve shifts downward
Q1 and P1 remain unchanged, but profit falls
P62G-MON-H-004.feedback: Fixed cost shifts ATC but does not change the MR=MC output.

P62G-MON-H-005.q: Refer to the graph. The demand price P1 currently lies above ATC at Q1. Suppose a higher fixed cost raises ATC exactly to P1 without changing demand, MR or MC. The monopoly would then earn:
options: Zero economic profit while covering all opportunity costs
Zero accounting profit necessarily
A loss equal to fixed cost
Positive profit because P1 exceeds MC
P62G-MON-H-005.feedback: The higher fixed cost raises ATC without moving the MR = MC output or demand price. When ATC reaches P1 at Q1, revenue covers all economic costs and economic profit becomes zero. The original plotted curves need not already show tangency.

P62G-MON-H-006.q: Refer to the graph. P1 is below ATC but above AVC at Q1. What should the monopolist do?
options: Shut down because P1 is below ATC
Produce Q1 and minimize its short-run loss
Raise price without changing quantity
Produce the competitive quantity
P62G-MON-H-006.feedback: Covering AVC and part of fixed cost reduces the loss.

P62G-MON-H-007.q: Refer to the graph. What is the monopolist’s total economic loss if the vertical gap between ATC and P1 is L?
options: One-half of L multiplied by Q1
The gap between P1 and MC multiplied by Q1
L multiplied by Q1
Fixed cost minus total revenue
P62G-MON-H-007.feedback: Loss is a rectangle: loss per unit times output.

P62G-MON-H-008.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the MR = MC rule remain relevant even when the monopolist is taking an economic loss?
options: It guarantees positive accounting profit
It identifies the shutdown price directly
It makes price equal marginal cost
It identifies the output that minimizes the loss, provided price covers AVC
P62G-MON-H-008.feedback: Marginal analysis chooses the best feasible output, not necessarily a profitable one.

P62G-MON-H-009.q: Refer to the graph. The best available price is below AVC. What should the monopolist do in the short run?
options: Produce zero in the short run
Produce Q1 because MR=MC
Produce where demand intersects MC
Ignore AVC because it has market power
P62G-MON-H-009.feedback: Price below AVC means revenue cannot cover avoidable cost.

P62G-MON-H-010.q: Refer to the graph. After short-run shutdown, which cost remains?
options: Variable cost of the unproduced units
Fixed cost
Marginal revenue
The deadweight-loss triangle
P62G-MON-H-010.feedback: Shutdown avoids variable cost but not short-run fixed cost.

P62G-MON-H-011.q: Refer to the graph. Q1 is monopoly output and Q2 is the D=MC quantity. The interval from Q1 to Q2 consists of units for which:
options: Marginal revenue exceeds demand
Average total cost is necessarily falling
Buyer willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost
Price discrimination is impossible
P62G-MON-H-011.feedback: Those omitted units would add to total surplus.

P62G-MON-H-012.q: Refer to the graph. Which area concept is created by restricting output from Q2 to Q1?
options: A transfer equal to all monopoly profit
Tariff revenue
Fixed cost
Deadweight loss from unrealized trades
P62G-MON-H-012.feedback: The restriction eliminates trades with positive net benefit.

P62G-MON-H-031.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, why is the price read from demand above marginal revenue?
options: An extra sale requires lowering price on earlier units
Marginal cost is already embedded in the downward demand curve
Average total cost must exceed marginal revenue at every output
The monopolist takes a fixed market price on all units sold
P62G-MON-H-031.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, expanding sales lowers the price received on previous units, so MR lies below price.

P62G-MON-H-032.q: Refer to the graph. Why would moving output from 36 toward 60 units reduce profit?
options: Demand exceeds ATC over the entire interval
Beyond Q = 36, MC exceeds MR
Price becomes greater than marginal revenue
ATC immediately becomes fixed cost
P62G-MON-H-032.feedback: Once output passes MR = MC, the additional units cost more at the margin than they add to revenue.

P62G-MON-H-034.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison correctly describes the monopoly outcome and the D = MC benchmark?
options: Monopoly: P = $30, Q = 60; benchmark: P = $42, Q = 36
Monopoly: P = $24, Q = 36; benchmark: P = $27, Q = 60
Monopoly and the benchmark both have P = $30 and Q = 60
Monopoly: P = $42, Q = 36; D = MC benchmark: P = $30, Q = 60
P62G-MON-H-034.feedback: The monopoly restricts output to 36 and charges $42; the D = MC benchmark is 60 units at $30.

P62G-MON-H-036.q: Refer to the graph. Why is Q = 67 not the profit-maximizing monopoly output?
options: At Q = 67, marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue
At Q = 67, price is greater than marginal cost
At Q = 67, ATC is necessarily zero
The monopolist must always choose the demand intercept
P62G-MON-H-036.feedback: A monopolist maximizes profit where MR = MC, not where demand equals MC.

P62G-MON-H-041.q: Refer to the graph. Which feature is consistent with a natural monopoly over the relevant range?
options: ATC declines as output expands toward the efficient quantity
MR is horizontal across the relevant output range
Demand becomes perfectly elastic near the efficient output
MC rises faster than demand throughout the relevant range
P62G-MON-H-041.feedback: Declining ATC over the relevant output range signals economies of scale that can support natural monopoly.

P62G-MON-H-043.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the fair-return outcome near Q = 116 and P = $16 imply approximately zero economic profit?
options: P = ATC at the fair-return output
P = MR at the fair-return output
MC = ATC at the $10 regulated price
Total revenue equals zero near Q = 116
P62G-MON-H-043.feedback: Average-cost pricing sets P = ATC, covering economic costs without positive economic profit.

P62G-MON-L-093.q: Refer to the graph. Which sequence best describes the monopoly outcome shown?
options: D = MC gives Q = 40; MR gives P = $20; P > ATC therefore creates economic profit
MR = ATC gives Q = 67; demand gives P = $27; the monopolist therefore breaks even
MR = MC gives Q = 40; demand gives P = $40; P < ATC causes a loss; D = MC is near Q = 67
MC = ATC gives Q = 40; demand gives P = $45; economic profit is therefore zero
P62G-MON-L-093.feedback: The graph separates the monopoly marginal decision, price read from demand, loss test against ATC, and efficient D = MC benchmark.

P62G-MON-L-094.q: Refer to the graph. What is the strongest reason a subsidy may be paired with marginal-cost pricing?
options: At efficient output, P = MC remains below ATC
At efficient output, P exceeds both MC and ATC
At monopoly output, price is already below marginal cost
A subsidy is needed to keep MR above demand at Q = 90
P62G-MON-L-094.feedback: A natural monopoly can be allocatively efficient at P = MC yet unable to cover total cost because ATC remains higher.

P62H-MCMP-B2-020.q: As entry erodes short-run profit, what zero-profit geometry characterizes the standard long-run equilibrium?
options: Demand is horizontal at minimum ATC
Demand is tangent to ATC and economic profit is zero
Price equals MC and ATC
MR is tangent to demand
P62H-MCMP-B2-020.feedback: Entry or exit continues until P=ATC at the chosen output.

P62H-MCMP-B3-039.q: Which welfare conclusion about Grove Coffee is safest?
options: Compare added consumer value or information with resource cost and market-power effects
All differentiation is wasteful
All advertising raises total surplus
Zero economic profit guarantees efficiency
P62H-MCMP-B3-039.feedback: Welfare requires a balanced comparison of benefits and costs.

options: All differentiation is wasteful

P62H-MCMP-B3-042.feedback: Welfare requires a balanced comparison of benefits and costs.

options: All differentiation is wasteful

P62H-MCMP-B3-045.feedback: Welfare requires a balanced comparison of benefits and costs.

options: All differentiation is wasteful
Compare added consumer value or information with resource cost and market-power effects

P62H-MCMP-B3-048.feedback: Welfare requires a balanced comparison of benefits and costs.

options: Compare added consumer value or information with resource cost and market-power effects

Zero economic profit guarantees efficiency
P62H-MCMP-B3-051.feedback: Welfare requires a balanced comparison of benefits and costs.
