options: All differentiation is wasteful
All advertising raises total surplus
Zero economic profit guarantees efficiency
Compare added consumer value or information with resource cost and market-power effects
P62H-MCMP-B3-054.feedback: Welfare requires a balanced comparison of benefits and costs.

P62H-MCMP-B3-055.q: Refer to the graph. The firm produces Q = 36 while efficient scale is Q = 50. Which conclusion best describes the long-run outcome?
options: The firm has 14 units of excess capacity and positive economic profit
The firm has 14 units of excess capacity while earning zero economic profit
The firm is productively efficient because P equals ATC
The firm is allocatively efficient because entry has occurred
P62H-MCMP-B3-055.feedback: The firm earns zero profit because P = ATC at Q = 36, but efficient scale is Q = 50, leaving 14 units of excess capacity.

P62H-MCMP-EL-016.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=20, minimum-ATC output Q2=34.64, price $70.00 and MC=$50.00. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $50.00; excess capacity 20 units.
Markup $20.00; excess capacity 14.64 units.
Markup $20.00; excess capacity 34.64 units.
Markup $70.00; excess capacity 14.64 units.
P62H-MCMP-EL-016.feedback: Markup is P−MC=70.00−50.00=$20.00. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=34.64−20=14.64 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-EL-017.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the firm not expand from Q1 toward Q2 even though ATC would fall?
options: The firm cannot physically produce beyond Q1 because excess capacity is a binding production limit
Price would automatically equal MC
Beyond Q1, marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue under its current demand
Entry is legally prohibited
P62H-MCMP-EL-017.feedback: Profit maximization, not minimum ATC alone, determines output.
P62H-MCMP-EL-017.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=20 and Q2=34.64. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-EL-017.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=20, D and ATC meet at P1=70; MR and MC meet at 50. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=34.64.

P62H-MCMP-EL-018.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=24, minimum-ATC output Q2=42.93, price $76.00 and MC=$49.60. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $49.60; excess capacity 24 units.
Markup $26.40; excess capacity 42.93 units.
Markup $76.00; excess capacity 18.93 units.
Markup $26.40; excess capacity 18.93 units.
P62H-MCMP-EL-018.feedback: Markup is P−MC=76.00−49.60=$26.40. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=42.93−24=18.93 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-EL-020.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=18, minimum-ATC output Q2=30.12, price $64.00 and MC=$47.80. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $47.80; excess capacity 18 units.
Markup $16.20; excess capacity 12.12 units.
Markup $16.20; excess capacity 30.12 units.
Markup $64.00; excess capacity 12.12 units.
P62H-MCMP-EL-020.feedback: Markup is P−MC=64.00−47.80=$16.20. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=30.12−18=12.12 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-EL-021.q: Refer to the graph. Why does P = ATC at Q1 not imply allocative efficiency?
options: Price still exceeds marginal cost at Q1
Price is below average variable cost at Q1
Marginal revenue exceeds demand at Q1
Output exceeds efficient scale at Q1
P62H-MCMP-EL-021.feedback: P = ATC establishes zero economic profit, but allocative efficiency requires P = MC; the graph shows P > MC.
P62H-MCMP-EL-021.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=18 and Q2=30.12. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-EL-021.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=18, D and ATC meet at P1=64; MR and MC meet at 47.8. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=30.12.

P62H-MCMP-EL-022.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=28, minimum-ATC output Q2=51.63, price $82.00 and MC=$48.40. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $48.40; excess capacity 28 units.
Markup $33.60; excess capacity 51.63 units.
Markup $82.00; excess capacity 23.63 units.
Markup $33.60; excess capacity 23.63 units.
P62H-MCMP-EL-022.feedback: Markup is P−MC=82.00−48.40=$33.60. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=51.63−28=23.63 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-EL-023.q: Refer to the graph. If firms are earning short-run profit before reaching the long-run tangency shown, which effect of entry moves the market toward that outcome?
options: Existing firms’ demand shifts left
Existing firms’ marginal cost shifts right
Industry demand becomes perfectly elastic
The minimum point of ATC shifts to Q1
P62H-MCMP-EL-023.feedback: Entry adds substitutes and shifts the demand curve facing each existing firm left until it is tangent to ATC.
P62H-MCMP-EL-023.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=28 and Q2=51.63. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-EL-023.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=28, D and ATC meet at P1=82; MR and MC meet at 48.4. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=51.63.

P62H-MCMP-EL-024.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=22, minimum-ATC output Q2=35.47, price $68.00 and MC=$50.40. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $50.40; excess capacity 22 units.
Markup $17.60; excess capacity 13.47 units.
Markup $17.60; excess capacity 35.47 units.
Markup $68.00; excess capacity 13.47 units.
P62H-MCMP-EL-024.feedback: Markup is P−MC=68.00−50.40=$17.60. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=35.47−22=13.47 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-EL-025.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the firm retain a positive markup despite earning zero economic profit?
options: Demand lies above marginal cost at Q1
Demand is tangent to marginal cost at Q2
Average total cost is vertical at Q1
Marginal revenue equals demand at every output
P62H-MCMP-EL-025.feedback: The downward-sloping demand curve gives a price above marginal cost at Q1 even though tangency with ATC makes economic profit zero.
P62H-MCMP-EL-025.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=22 and Q2=35.47. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-EL-025.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=22, D and ATC meet at P1=68; MR and MC meet at 50.4. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=35.47.

P62H-MCMP-EL-031.q: Refer to the graph. If the short-run outcome shown persists initially, what market adjustment is most consistent with monopolistic competition?
options: Exit shifts each incumbent firm’s demand right until price equals marginal cost
Entry shifts each incumbent firm’s marginal cost downward until price equals ATC
Entry shifts each incumbent firm’s demand left until economic profit is eliminated
No entry occurs because differentiated firms can earn permanent economic profit
P62H-MCMP-EL-031.feedback: Positive short-run profit attracts entry, which reduces the demand faced by each incumbent.

P62H-MCMP-EL-032.q: Refer to the graph. Which feature most directly shows allocative inefficiency at the firm’s chosen output?
options: Price of $37 exceeds ATC of $33 by $4
ATC of $33 exceeds marginal cost of $23 by $10
MR equals MC at $23 when quantity equals 50
Price of $37 exceeds marginal cost of $23
P62H-MCMP-EL-032.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires P = MC; here P exceeds MC by $14.

P62H-MCMP-EL-033.q: Refer to the graph. If the zero-profit outcome shown is a long-run equilibrium, what market force has already done its work?
options: Advertising has shifted firm demand until price equals marginal cost
A regulator has set price equal to average total cost at Q = 36
Collusion has eliminated rivalry and guaranteed zero economic profit
Entry or exit has adjusted firm demand until economic profit is zero
P62H-MCMP-EL-033.feedback: Long-run entry and exit shift each firm’s demand until P = ATC at the chosen output.

P62H-MCMP-EL-034.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement best captures the two inefficiencies shown?
options: The firm has P < MC and produces above the minimum-ATC quantity
The firm has P = MC but ATC exceeds price
The firm has P > MC and produces below the minimum-ATC quantity
The firm has MR = demand and produces at minimum ATC
P62H-MCMP-EL-034.feedback: P > MC indicates allocative inefficiency, and Q = 36 below efficient scale Q = 50 indicates productive inefficiency.

P62H-MCMP-EL-035.q: Refer to the graph. Compared with a profitable short-run position, what happened to the demand facing the incumbent as entry occurred?
options: It became perfectly horizontal at the quantity where ATC is minimized
It shifted outward until the firm produced where price equals marginal cost
It became identical to marginal revenue throughout the relevant output range
It shifted inward until it became tangent to ATC at the chosen output
P62H-MCMP-EL-035.feedback: Entry reduces each incumbent’s demand until the firm earns zero economic profit.

P62H-MCMP-EL-036.q: Refer to the graph. The firm could lower ATC by producing 50 units. Why is that not necessarily profit maximizing?
options: MR no longer equals MC at Q = 50 under the current demand curve
ATC cannot decline when a monopolistically competitive firm expands output
Producing 50 units would eliminate the firm’s product differentiation
Long-run equilibrium requires the firm to maximize use of physical capacity
P62H-MCMP-EL-036.feedback: Minimum ATC is not the firm’s objective; profit maximization still follows MR = MC.

P62H-MCMP-EL-037.q: Refer to the displayed long-run firm graph. A policymaker argues that because entry has eliminated economic profit, consumers cannot gain from additional mutually beneficial trades. Which response is economically sound?
options: P = ATC proves P = MC, so the policymaker’s inference is sound
P = ATC establishes zero profit, but P > MC still signals a markup; a policy must also consider differentiated-product benefits and cost recovery
The firm must earn positive economic profit because output is below minimum ATC
Free entry makes the firm a price taker, so the plotted downward-sloping demand is irrelevant
P62H-MCMP-EL-037.feedback: The graph combines P = ATC with P > MC and output below efficient scale. Entry removes profit without eliminating markup. The markup identifies a potential allocative issue, but the graph does not quantify the value of variety or the costs of a proposed remedy.

P62H-MCMP-H-013.q: Refer to the graph. Demand is tangent to ATC at Q1 = 20 and price $70. Which combination is correct?
options: Zero economic profit, positive markup, and excess capacity
Positive economic profit with production at minimum average total cost and price equal to marginal cost
Zero markup and allocative efficiency
Economic loss and immediate exit
P62H-MCMP-H-013.feedback: Tangency gives P=ATC, while P>MC and Q is below minimum ATC.
P62H-MCMP-H-013.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=20 and Q2=34.64. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-H-013.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=20, D and ATC meet at P1=70; MR and MC meet at 50. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=34.64.

P62H-MCMP-H-014.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose the firm’s demand shifts outward while costs are unchanged. What is the immediate short-run effect?
options: The firm must earn zero profit immediately
The firm can earn economic profit, encouraging entry
Existing-firm demand shifts left immediately because entry occurs before the outward demand change
The minimum-ATC quantity falls automatically
P62H-MCMP-H-014.feedback: An outward demand shift can create short-run profit before entry responds.
P62H-MCMP-H-014.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=20 and Q2=34.64. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-H-014.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=20, D and ATC meet at P1=70; MR and MC meet at 50. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=34.64.

P62H-MCMP-H-015.q: Refer to the graph. Which equality at Q1 establishes that the firm earns zero economic profit?
options: Price equals average total cost
Price equals marginal cost
Marginal revenue equals average total cost
Average total cost equals minimum average variable cost
P62H-MCMP-H-015.feedback: The demand curve is tangent to ATC at Q1, so price equals average total cost and economic profit is zero.
P62H-MCMP-H-015.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=24 and Q2=42.93. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-H-015.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=24, D and ATC meet at P1=76; MR and MC meet at 49.6. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=42.93.

P62H-MCMP-H-016.q: Refer to the graph. After short-run profit induces entry, what happens to the demand curve facing an existing firm?
options: It shifts left until it is tangent to ATC
It shifts right until price equals marginal cost
It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It remains fixed while marginal cost shifts left
P62H-MCMP-H-016.feedback: Entry provides more substitutes and shifts each existing firm’s demand left until tangency restores zero economic profit.
P62H-MCMP-H-016.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=24 and Q2=42.93. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-H-016.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=24, D and ATC meet at P1=76; MR and MC meet at 49.6. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=42.93.

P62H-MCMP-H-017.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison at Q1 demonstrates allocative inefficiency?
options: Price exceeds marginal cost
Price equals marginal cost
Price is below average variable cost
Marginal revenue exceeds price
P62H-MCMP-H-017.feedback: At Q1 the demand curve gives price above marginal cost, so the allocative-efficiency condition P = MC is not met.
P62H-MCMP-H-017.imageAlt: Demand, marginal revenue and cost curves with Q1=18 and Q2=30.12. See graph description for coordinates.
P62H-MCMP-H-017.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. D=AR slopes downward and MR lies below it. At Q1=18, D and ATC meet at P1=64; MR and MC meet at 47.8. ATC is U-shaped. MC crosses ATC at its minimum, marked Q2=30.12.

P62H-MCMP-H-018.q: Refer to the graph. Once entry restores long-run equilibrium, which combination can still persist?
options: Zero economic profit with a positive markup
Positive economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
A shutdown loss with minimum average total cost
Zero economic profit with no excess capacity

P62H-MCMP-H-021.q: A costly brand campaign shifts demand right but also makes demand less elastic. Which conclusion is safest?

Profit must rise
Price must fall
Marginal cost must remain above marginal revenue at every possible quantity after the campaign
P62H-MCMP-H-021.feedback: Demand and cost effects must be evaluated together.

P62H-MCMP-H-032.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the firm’s price read from the demand curve rather than from the MR = MC intersection?
options: Price is read from demand after output is chosen where MR = MC
Price must equal marginal cost at the profit-maximizing output
The firm chooses price where ATC intersects marginal cost
The $23 value is the price consumers pay on the demand curve
P62H-MCMP-H-032.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, the firm chooses Q where MR = MC and then reads price from demand.

P62H-MCMP-H-034.q: Refer to the graph. Why is zero economic profit consistent with the firm continuing to operate?
options: Revenue covers all explicit and implicit economic costs
Zero economic profit means the firm receives no revenue
The firm continues only because price equals marginal cost
The firm must be subsidized whenever economic profit is zero
P62H-MCMP-H-034.feedback: P = ATC means the firm covers all economic costs, including normal return.

P62H-MCMP-H-036.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement best distinguishes the displayed outcome from a perfectly competitive long-run equilibrium?
options: A competitive firm also faces a downward-sloping demand curve
A competitive firm sets MR below price at its chosen output
The firm can have P = ATC while still having P > MC
Perfect competition requires economic profit to remain positive
P62H-MCMP-H-036.feedback: Monopolistic competition can have zero economic profit with a markup because firm demand slopes downward.

P62H-MCMP-H-037.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the firm not expand from Q = 36 to the efficient scale of Q = 50?
options: The firm is physically unable to produce more than 36 units
Price would rise automatically if output increased to 50
Marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost at every output above 36
Profit maximization is governed by MR = MC, not by minimizing ATC alone
P62H-MCMP-H-037.feedback: The firm stops at MR = MC even though ATC would be lower at a larger output.

P62H-MCMP-H-038.q: Refer to the graph. Which pair of facts demonstrates long-run zero economic profit and productive inefficiency?
options: P = ATC at Q = 36, while minimum ATC occurs at Q = 50
P = MC at Q = 36, while ATC is constant after Q = 50
MR = demand at Q = 36, while MC is minimized at Q = 50
P exceeds ATC at Q = 36, while MR equals zero at Q = 50
P62H-MCMP-H-038.feedback: P = ATC gives zero economic profit, while Q below the minimum-ATC output creates excess capacity.

P62H-MCMP-H-039.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the long-run outcome not allocatively efficient?
options: Price of $27 equals ATC at the chosen quantity of 36
Price of $27 exceeds marginal cost of $15.50 at Q = 36
ATC reaches its minimum of $25 at the efficient scale of 50
Demand is tangent to ATC at the long-run quantity of 36
P62H-MCMP-H-039.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires P = MC, but here price exceeds marginal cost by $11.50.

P62H-MCMP-L-032.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=20, minimum-ATC output Q2=34.64, price $70.00 and MC=$50.00. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?

Markup $20.00; excess capacity 34.64 units.
Markup $70.00; excess capacity 14.64 units.
Markup $20.00; excess capacity 14.64 units.
P62H-MCMP-L-032.feedback: Markup is P−MC=70.00−50.00=$20.00. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=34.64−20=14.64 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-L-035.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=24, minimum-ATC output Q2=42.93, price $76.00 and MC=$49.60. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?

Markup $26.40; excess capacity 42.93 units.
Markup $26.40; excess capacity 18.93 units.
Markup $76.00; excess capacity 18.93 units.
P62H-MCMP-L-035.feedback: Markup is P−MC=76.00−49.60=$26.40. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=42.93−24=18.93 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-L-038.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=18, minimum-ATC output Q2=30.12, price $64.00 and MC=$47.80. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?

Markup $16.20; excess capacity 30.12 units.

P62H-MCMP-L-038.feedback: Markup is P−MC=64.00−47.80=$16.20. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=30.12−18=12.12 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-L-041.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=28, minimum-ATC output Q2=51.63, price $82.00 and MC=$48.40. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?

P62H-MCMP-L-044.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has chosen output Q1=22, minimum-ATC output Q2=35.47, price $68.00 and MC=$50.40. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?

P62H-MCMP-L-091.q: Refer to the graph. If entry eliminates the short-run profit shown while the firm remains monopolistically competitive, which long-run condition should emerge?

Demand becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
MR becomes identical to demand at every output
Price falls below AVC so every incumbent shuts down
P62H-MCMP-L-091.feedback: Long-run entry shifts the firm’s demand until P = ATC at the profit-maximizing quantity while demand remains downward sloping.

P62H-MCMP-L-092.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement best evaluates the claim that zero economic profit makes the firm both productively and allocatively efficient?
options: Zero profit alone proves neither minimum ATC production nor P = MC
The student is correct whenever P equals ATC
Only productive efficiency fails; allocative efficiency follows from zero profit
Only allocative efficiency fails; productive efficiency follows from zero profit
P62H-MCMP-L-092.feedback: Zero economic profit is not an efficiency test. The graph still has a downward-sloping demand curve and P > MC.

P62H-MCMP-L-093.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose a policy forced price down to marginal cost at Q = 36 without changing costs. What tension would arise?
options: Economic profit would rise because price would equal marginal cost
ATC would automatically fall to $15.50 at Q = 36
The firm would no longer cover the $27 ATC shown at that output
Excess capacity would disappear because Q would remain 36
P62H-MCMP-L-093.feedback: At Q = 36, MC is $15.50 while ATC and current price are $27; forcing P to MC would put price below ATC.

P62H-MCMP-L-094.q: Refer to the graph. After short-run profit attracts entry, which sequence correctly describes the adjustment toward long-run equilibrium?
options: Entry shifts incumbent demand outward; markup disappears; output reaches minimum ATC
Entry lowers marginal cost; demand becomes horizontal; positive profit remains
Entry raises average total cost; price falls below AVC; all incumbents exit
Entry shifts incumbent demand inward; profit falls to zero; output stays below minimum ATC
P62H-MCMP-L-094.feedback: Entry shifts each incumbent’s demand inward until zero profit, while product differentiation leaves a downward-sloping demand curve and excess capacity.

P62H-MCMP-L-095.q: Refer to the long-run monopolistic-competition graph. A proposal would force each firm to produce at minimum ATC while also pricing at MC. Which assessment uses the diagram and recognizes what it cannot establish about welfare?
options: The current markup is $11.50 and excess capacity is 14 units; policy evaluation must also weigh lost variety and cost recovery, which the firm diagram does not measure
The current $11.50 markup is economic profit, so eliminating it necessarily leaves every variety financially viable
Current zero profit proves efficient output, so neither the markup nor product variety belongs in welfare analysis
Excess capacity is 14 units of unsold inventory, so ordering its sale necessarily raises total consumer welfare
P62H-MCMP-L-095.feedback: At Q = 36, P = ATC = $27 while MC = $15.50, giving an $11.50 markup. Minimum ATC occurs at Q = 50, so excess capacity is 14 units, not inventory. Producing more at a mandated price is not automatically feasible at zero profit. Buyers may value differentiation; the diagram alone cannot quantify the benefits of variety or the policy’s net welfare effect.

P62I-OLI-L-004.q: Refer to the payoff matrix for a port-services coordination review. Payoffs are profits ordered (Row, Column). Comparing both players’ best responses with the sum of their payoffs, which conclusion is supported?
options: B/Y is the only pure equilibrium because Column prefers its payoff there
A/X is the only pure equilibrium because it has the largest joint total
Neither diagonal cell is an equilibrium because the off-diagonal totals are lower
A/X and B/Y are pure equilibria; A/X has the larger joint total, 23 versus 21
P62I-OLI-L-004.feedback: Against X, Row chooses A; against Y, Row chooses B. Against A, Column chooses X; against B, Column chooses Y. Both diagonal cells are equilibria, with joint totals 23 and 21. Neither player has a dominant strategy. The maximum joint-profit cell is also one equilibrium; it need not be the selected outcome.

P62I-OLI-L-010.q: Refer to the payoff matrix for a rotating delivery-slot game. Payoffs are profits ordered (Row, Column). Comparing both players’ best responses with the sum of their payoffs, which conclusion is supported?
options: There are four pure-strategy equilibria because all four joint totals equal 8
There is no pure-strategy equilibrium; all four cells tie at a joint total of 8
A/X is the unique equilibrium because Row receives 6 there
B/Y is the joint optimum because Column receives 2 there
P62I-OLI-L-010.feedback: Row chooses A against X and B against Y. Column chooses Y against A and X against B. Every pure cell permits a profitable deviation. Each cell totals 8, so equal joint profit does not create a pure equilibrium. A mixed-strategy equilibrium is distinct from a pure one.

P62I-OLI-L-072.q: Two rival cruise lines keep fares at $72 and sell 30 units each in the kinked-demand model shown. Rivals match fare cuts but do not match fare increases. A per-unit cost increase raises this firm’s constant MC from $48 to $54, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. How do its profit-maximizing fare, quantity and economic profit change?
options: Fare rises to $78 and quantity stays at 30; economic profit is unchanged.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit is unchanged because MR has a gap.
Fare falls and quantity rises; economic profit falls by less than $180.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit falls by $180.
P62I-OLI-L-072.feedback: At Q=30 the MR gap runs from $36 to $60. Both MC=$48 and MC=$54 fall inside it, so the optimum remains at the kink, P=$72 and Q=30. Cost rises $6 on each of 30 units, lowering profit by $180.

P62I-OLI-L-073.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown: P=70−0.5Q up to Q=20 and P=90−1.5Q above Q=20. Its constant MC initially equals $40. Compare a rise in MC to $45 with a rise to $55, holding demand fixed. Which conclusion is correct?
options: At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50.
At MC=$45 and MC=$55 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60 because any cost change lies inside the MR gap.
At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it expands output to Q=25 and lowers price to $52.50.
At MC=$45 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50; at MC=$55 it returns to Q=20 and P=$60.
P62I-OLI-L-073.feedback: At the kink MR drops from $50 to $30. MC=$45 lies within that range, but MC=$55 lies above it. On the upper demand branch MR=70−Q, so 70−Q=55 gives Q=15 and P=70−0.5×15=$62.50.
P62I-OLI-L-073.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 20, price 60, with two MR branches and MC at 40.
P62I-OLI-L-073.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=70−0.5Q for Q up to 20, then P=90−1.5Q for larger Q. At Q=20, the upper MR branch ends at 50 and the lower branch begins at 30. MC is horizontal at 40.

P62I-OLI-L-074.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown, with prevailing price $72, quantity 30 and constant MC=$48. An input improvement lowers MC to $42, while a recurring license fee adds $300 to fixed cost. Demand does not change. Which evaluation correctly separates the output decision from the profit effect?
options: Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving exceeds the $300 fee, so economic profit rises by $120.
Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the $300 fee, so economic profit falls by $120.
The fixed fee raises MC above the MR gap, so quantity falls; the variable-cost saving cannot affect profit.
The lower MC moves quantity above the kink; the fixed fee is a variable cost, so profit is unchanged.
P62I-OLI-L-074.feedback: The MR gap at Q=30 is $36 to $60; MC=$42 remains inside it, so P and Q stay at $72 and 30. Variable cost falls by ($48−$42)×30=$180. The $300 fixed fee does not enter MC but exceeds that saving, reducing profit by $120.
P62I-OLI-L-074.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 30, price 72, with two MR branches and MC at 48.
P62I-OLI-L-074.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=84−0.4Q for Q up to 30, then P=108−1.2Q for larger Q. At Q=30, the upper MR branch ends at 60 and the lower branch begins at 36. MC is horizontal at 48.

P62I-OLI-LB-007.q: Use the displayed payoff matrix as the baseline. A coordination program adds 6 to each firm’s payoff only at (A,X), leaving all other cells unchanged. Which list contains all pure-strategy Nash equilibria after the change, and which outcome maximizes joint payoff?
options: Both (A,X) and (B,Y) are equilibria; (A,X) maximizes joint payoff at 32.
Only (A,X) is an equilibrium; improving that cell removes the incentive to choose B against Y.
Only (B,Y) is an equilibrium; the added payoff cannot alter any best response.
Both (A,Y) and (B,X) are equilibria; their unequal payoffs maximize the joint total.
P62I-OLI-LB-007.feedback: The new (A,X) payoff is (16,16), so A is preferred to B against X and X to Y against A. Against Y, row still prefers B (7>5), and against B, column still prefers Y (7>5). Thus the old (B,Y) equilibrium also remains, while (A,X) yields the highest joint payoff.

P62I-OLI-LB-021.q: Use the cartel graph with demand P=100−2Q and MC=$20. Two identical cartel members split the joint-profit-maximizing output equally. One secretly produces one additional unit while its rival holds its quota. Which comparison explains the incentive conflict?
options: The deviator’s profit falls from $400 to $398, while combined profit rises from $800 to $818.
Both member and joint profit rise because an extra unit always sells above marginal cost.
The deviator’s profit rises from $400 to $418, while combined profit falls from $800 to $798.
Neither profit changes because the original quota was jointly optimal.
P62I-OLI-LB-021.feedback: Joint MR=100−4Q equals 20 at Q=20, P=60; each supplies 10 for profit $400. Deviation makes total Q=21 and P=58; the deviator earns (58−20)×11=$418. Combined profit is (58−20)×21=$798.

P62I-OLI-LB-024.q: Use the cartel graph with demand P=140−2.5Q and MC=$30. Two members split cartel output equally. One adds two units while the other holds its quota. Which current-profit comparison and deterrence threshold are correct, ignoring other effects?
options: The deviator loses $10 while combined profit gains $45; any positive punishment is unnecessary.
The deviator gains $45 while combined profit falls $10; an expected present-value punishment greater than $45 deters this deviation.
The deviator gains $110 and combined profit rises $110; a punishment below $45 is sufficient.
The deviator gains $45 and combined profit is unchanged; joint optimization guarantees no harm to its rival.
P62I-OLI-LB-024.feedback: Joint optimum is Q=22, P=85, with 11 units and $605 profit per member. Deviation gives total Q=24, P=80; the deviator supplies 13 for $650, a $45 gain. Total profit changes from $1210 to $1200. Compare the $45 gain with the discounted expected future penalty.

P62I-OLI-LB-027.q: Use the cartel graph with demand P=100−2Q and MC=$20. Compare a $200 lump-sum license charge on the cartel with a $10 tax per unit. The cartel stays active and reoptimizes jointly. Which comparison is correct?
options: The license leaves Q=20 and P=$60 with net profit $600; the per-unit tax gives Q=17.5 and P=$65 with net profit $612.50.
Both policies leave Q=20 and P=$60 because all taxes are fixed costs.
The license reduces output to 17.5, while the per-unit tax leaves output 20 because its payment is a transfer.
Both policies increase output to 40 because taxes force price to equal the original MC.
P62I-OLI-LB-027.feedback: The license leaves MR=MC unchanged and subtracts $200 from original profit $800. The unit tax raises effective MC to $30: 100−4Q=30 gives Q=17.5 and P=65, with net operating profit (65−30)×17.5=$612.50.

PG1-SUP-L-001.q: Refer to the graph. A producer says the move from A to B proves that supply increased by 125 thousand units. What is the correct diagnosis?

A and B show a leftward shift of the supply curve.
The higher quantity means the demand curve shifted right.
It is more quantity supplied, not an increase in supply.
PG1-SUP-L-001.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied along a fixed supply curve. A supply increase would require a rightward shift of the entire curve.

PMC-COP-R-010.q: A learner says, “If the owner did not write a check, the resource has no cost.
options: Only variable resources have economic costs
Every implicit cost must appear on an invoice
Opportunity cost matters only for consumers
Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
PMC-COP-R-010.feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

PMC-COP-R-025.q: A learner calls zero economic profit a “loss.

Zero economic profit means revenue is zero
Zero economic profit means explicit costs exceed revenue
Zero economic profit excludes owner compensation
PMC-COP-R-025.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost, so zero economic profit can be a sustainable outcome.

PMC-COP-R-068.q: A learner says AFC eventually rises because “all U-shaped costs rise.
options: AFC rises whenever MC rises
AFC keeps falling as fixed cost is spread over more output
AFC is U-shaped like AVC
AFC equals MC at its minimum
PMC-COP-R-068.feedback: AFC is not U-shaped in the standard model; it declines as quantity increases.

PMC-COP-R-117.q: A learner says, “Fixed cost and sunk cost mean the same thing.
options: A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
Every sunk cost varies with output
Every fixed cost has already been paid forever
Sunk costs are always implicit
PMC-COP-R-117.feedback: Fixed describes how cost behaves with current output; sunk describes whether it can be recovered.

PMS-ELAS-R-029.q: A learner says labor demand elasticity is unrelated to substitution possibilities. Best correction?
options: More available substitutes for a type of labor generally make labor demand more elastic
Substitutes make labor demand perfectly inelastic
Factor demand elasticity depends only on worker preferences
Substitution changes labor supply but never labor demand
PMS-ELAS-R-029.feedback: Employers can respond more strongly to wage changes when alternative inputs are available.
